messages.subject: A question about Lod score
parts:
I have a question about Lod Score

In an intercross, we use ANOVA and gives an F statistic, and there is a relationship between F and LOD score.

My question is, in case of ANOVA, there are three conditions we need to consider
  • Independence of observations
  • Normality – the distributions of the residuals are normal.
  • Equality (or "homogeneity") of variances, called homoscedasticity
When I use ANOVA, with R, the command "shapiro.test" et "barlett.test" help do these things. But how can we verify these conditions in Lod Score?

Thank you

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A question about Lod score
parts:
The LOD score is equivalent to the F statistic from ANOVA.  See the attached page from the R/qtl book (http://www.rql.org/book).

- Independence is really important, but is not easily tested.  The most common departure is some sort of population structure (such as unequal relationships, as arises from having sibships in an AIL population.

- normality tends not to be terribly important; QTL analysis is remarkably robust, but you need to be sure to use a permutation test to determine significance.  Tests of normality tend not to be too useful, as it's the residual variation that is assumed to be normally distributed.  The marginal phenotype distribution follows a mixture of normals.

- departure from homoscedasticity can have a big effect on power.  I usually look at a histogram of the phenotypes and consider taking logs of square-roots.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A question about Lod score
parts:
>
> Can I say because of the formula of LOD score, I avoid the problem of "homoscedasticity"?
No; I think there's no difference from ANOVA generally.

>
> And another problem of statistic... Could you tell me how you can see the "homoscedasticity" from a histogram of phenotype? At university, we plot " qq-plot " of the residual for verifying this condition, so I don't know much about histogram. And I have no idea to plot a "qq-plot" for LOD score...
In my experience, non-constant variance usually goes with skewed distribution, so that's usually what I look for.

>
> And if these three conditions can't satisfy and the phenotype is not normality, we use non-normal phenotype, Is that right?
>

Even if the normality or constant-variance assumptions are violated, the standard analysis can still work fine, to detect QTL.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A question about Lod score
parts:
Generally you don't go far wrong with standard interval mapping, in spite of departures from normality and constant variance.  Or a simple transformation can suffice.  But rank-based methods can also be useful, eg when there are outliers, though I don't generally see much difference.

karl
